rw: Globalization means economies becoming increasingly linked through trade, investment, finance and the movement of ideas, so countries depend on one another more than before.

ww.The ban on trading with other countries: A ban on trading with other countries is the opposite of globalization, which is defined by expanding cross-border exchange and deepening ties between nations.
ww.The merger of all countries into one nat: Globalization does not merge countries into one nation; each keeps its own government, borders and laws while becoming more connected through trade and investment.
ww.The growth of a single country's local m: Globalization is about links between many economies, so growth of one country's local market alone describes domestic expansion rather than any worldwide integration.

rw: Countries trade mainly to obtain goods that other nations can make at lower cost or that they cannot produce well at home, which raises living standards.

ww.To avoid using money at all in their tra: Trade does not avoid money; payments still happen in currencies, and barter is only a rare side case, so this is not the reason countries trade.
ww.To prevent other nations from growing st: Trade is generally mutually beneficial, so preventing others from growing stronger is not its purpose, and hurting partners would also shrink the gains the country itself enjoys.
ww.To raise their own prices at home and ab: Countries do not trade to raise their own prices; trade usually lowers prices by adding supply and competition, so higher prices at home are not the motive.

rw: When each producer focuses on what it does best and trades, total output rises and competition and efficiency push prices lower for buyers everywhere.

ww.Less cooperation between nations: Specialization and trade increase cooperation between nations rather than reducing it, so less cooperation is the reverse of what actually happens when countries exchange goods.
ww.Higher import taxes for all countries: Higher import taxes are a barrier that restricts trade, and they are not a benefit of specialization, which works by letting goods cross borders more freely.
ww.Fewer choices for consumers overall: Trade gives consumers more choices by bringing in foreign varieties, so fewer choices is backwards; the typical result is wider selection and better goods.

rw: Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost is lower: A in cloth and B in wheat, then trade, so both consume more than they could alone.

ww.Neither should trade with the other coun: If neither trades, each country gives up the gains from its lower opportunity cost, so both end up with less cloth and wheat than trading would give.
ww.Each country should make both goods alon: Making both goods alone ignores comparative advantage, so each country wastes resources on the good it makes at higher opportunity cost, leaving both with smaller total output.
ww.A makes wheat and B makes cloth, and the: A making wheat and B making cloth reverses comparative advantage, since A is better at cloth and B at wheat, so this plan would raise costs for both.

rw: An exchange rate states how much of one currency is needed to buy a unit of another, such as dollars per euro, which links prices across countries.

ww.The tax on foreign goods at the border p: A tax on foreign goods at the border is a tariff, which raises the price of imports but is not what an exchange rate measures.
ww.The interest rate on foreign loans from: The interest rate on foreign loans is a borrowing cost set by lenders, whereas an exchange rate is a price that converts one currency into another.
ww.The fee for shipping goods overseas by s: A fee for shipping goods overseas is a transport cost added to trade, which is unrelated to the price at which currencies are swapped.

rw: When the dollar strengthens, each dollar buys more euros, so European goods cost fewer dollars and imports from Europe become cheaper for Americans.

ww.Free of all tariffs: A stronger dollar does not remove tariffs; tariffs are set by governments, and currency moves change only the dollar price of foreign goods, not the taxes on them.
ww.Pricier for Americans: Pricier would be the result of a weaker dollar, where each dollar buys fewer euros; a stronger dollar does the opposite and lowers the dollar cost of imports.
ww.Impossible to buy: Imports do not become impossible to buy; a stronger dollar actually makes European goods more affordable for Americans, so purchases would tend to rise rather than stop.

rw: Outsourcing means hiring another company, often in another country, to do work such as manufacturing or customer service instead of the firm doing that work itself.

ww.Producing all goods inside the company: Producing all goods inside the company is the opposite of outsourcing, which hands tasks to outside firms, so this describes keeping work in-house.
ww.Selling shares of stock to the public: Selling shares of stock to the public is an initial public offering or equity raise, a way of financing the firm rather than contracting out work.
ww.Building a new factory at home now: Building a new factory at home is domestic investment in the firm's own capacity, not outsourcing, which relies on an outside company to perform tasks.

rw: Offshoring means a company relocates some of its business operations, such as production or services, to another country, often to cut costs like labor.

ww.Moving operations to another city at hom: Moving operations to another city at home is relocation within the same country, whereas offshoring specifically means shifting work across national borders to a foreign location.
ww.Closing down a business permanently for: Closing a business permanently is a shutdown, which ends operations altogether, while offshoring keeps the business running but moves some of its activity abroad.
ww.Merging with a rival firm at home to cut: Merging with a rival at home is a consolidation of two firms, which says nothing about moving operations abroad, so it does not match offshoring.

rw: A trade bloc is a group of countries that agree to cut tariffs and other trade barriers among themselves, like the EU or USMCA.

ww.A group of companies that fix prices: A group of companies that fix prices is a cartel, which is an illegal or restrictive arrangement among firms and not a trade bloc of countries.
ww.A group of banks that lend to government: A group of banks lending to governments is a lending syndicate, a financial arrangement unrelated to countries agreeing on trade rules among themselves.
ww.A group of workers that bargains for pay: A group of workers bargaining for pay is a labor union, which negotiates wages and conditions rather than coordinating trade policy between nations.

rw: The WTO exists to keep trade flowing smoothly through agreed rules and to settle disputes between member countries, giving a forum for resolving trade conflicts.

ww.To set the price of oil each month: Setting the monthly price of oil is not the WTO's role; oil prices come from markets and producer decisions, such as those of OPEC.
ww.To lend money to poor countries or firms: Lending money to poor countries is the work of institutions such as the World Bank or IMF, not the WTO, which focuses on trade rules.
ww.To collect taxes from all nations: The WTO does not collect taxes from nations; it is funded by member contributions and has no power to tax, so this misstates its purpose.

rw: A cartel is a group of producers that agree to restrict output or fix prices, acting like a monopoly to raise profits at buyers' expense.

ww.A group of consumers that boycott a prod: A group of consumers boycotting a product is a boycott or consumer movement, which acts on the demand side, whereas a cartel is formed by producers.
ww.A government agency that regulates trade: A government agency regulating trade is a regulator, which enforces rules, while a cartel is a private arrangement among producers that often breaks competition laws.
ww.A group of workers in a trade union or g: A group of workers in a trade union or guild is a labor organization that bargains for pay, and it is not an agreement among producers on prices or output.

rw: The balance of payments records all money flowing into and out of a country from trade, services, investment and transfers, over a given period.

ww.A record of a company's yearly profit: A company's yearly profit is recorded on an income statement, which tracks one firm's earnings and has nothing to do with a nation's payments with the world.
ww.A list of taxes paid by citizens: A list of taxes paid by citizens is a tax record, while the balance of payments covers all transactions between a country and the rest of the world.
ww.A statement of government debt only: Government debt alone is a fiscal measure of public borrowing, while the balance of payments covers private and public flows of goods, services and capital with other nations.

rw: A car company building a factory abroad is foreign direct investment because it creates lasting physical ownership and control of productive assets in another country.

ww.A tourist buying a souvenir abroad: A tourist buying a souvenir is a small consumer purchase that creates no lasting ownership or control of business assets, so it is not direct investment.
ww.A bank lending money for one year only: A one-year bank loan is a short-term lending flow with no ownership or control of a foreign business, so it does not count as direct investment.
ww.A company paying a customs duty to a por: A company paying a customs duty to a port is paying a trade tax on goods, which is a cost of importing and not an investment.

rw: A trade barrier is a government measure, such as a tariff, quota or strict standard, that makes importing or exporting goods harder or more costly.

ww.A river that crosses a border or a town: A river crossing a border is a geographic feature, which might affect transport but is not a government measure and so is not a trade barrier.
ww.A contract between two exporters on sale: A contract between two exporters is a private sales agreement that does not restrict trade between countries, so it fails to be a trade barrier.
ww.A discount for foreign buyers of goods: A discount for foreign buyers makes foreign goods cheaper and trade easier, which is the opposite of a barrier that restricts or burdens trade.

rw: A strict product standard for imports restricts foreign sellers without using a tax, so it is a non-tariff barrier because it raises the difficulty of selling.

ww.A free trade agreement among nations: A free trade agreement lowers barriers and so is the opposite of a barrier; it also works by cutting tariffs, not by adding non-tariff limits.
ww.A lower tax for exporters, a subsidy: A subsidy lowers costs for domestic exporters and is a support payment rather than a restriction on imports, so it is not a non-tariff barrier.
ww.A tax on imported goods at the border: A tax on imported goods at the border is a tariff, which is by definition a tariff barrier rather than a non-tariff one.

rw: Protectionism is a set of policies, such as tariffs and quotas, that shield home industries from foreign competition by making imports costlier or harder to bring in.

ww.Government policies that remove all trad: Policies removing all trade barriers describe free trade, the opposite of protectionism, which adds barriers to defend domestic producers from foreign rivals.
ww.Government spending on defense and secur: Spending on defense and security is military policy and has no direct link to shielding home industries from import competition, so it is not protectionism.
ww.Government rules that protect consumers: Rules protecting consumers from fraud are consumer protection laws that regulate sellers, while protectionism concerns shielding domestic producers from foreign competition.

rw: Supporters argue that tariffs and quotas protect domestic jobs in industries that would otherwise lose business to cheaper foreign competition, which is the common case made.

ww.It lowers prices by keeping out cheap go: Lower prices from keeping out cheap goods is false; blocking cheap imports raises prices, so this is not an argument that supporters of protectionism can honestly make.
ww.It encourages more imports from abroad t: Protectionism aims to reduce imports, not encourage them, so encouraging more imports from abroad contradicts its purpose and cannot be its main argument.
ww.It improves variety for buyers in the ma: Better variety for buyers is a benefit of open trade, since imports add choices, while protectionism usually narrows the range of goods on offer.

rw: Critics say protectionism raises prices for consumers because competition falls, and that other countries may retaliate with their own barriers, harming exporters.

ww.It lowers the cost of imports for buyers: Lowering the cost of imports for buyers is a benefit of free trade, so it cannot be a criticism of protectionism, which does the reverse.
ww.It always creates more jobs for the nati: Protectionism does not always create more jobs; it may save some jobs but costs others when prices rise or exporters face retaliation, so always is false.
ww.It increases competition abroad for loca: Protection reduces competition from abroad for local firms, so it would not increase it, and that reduced competition is part of why critics oppose it.

rw: A free trade agreement is a treaty in which member countries cut or remove tariffs and other trade barriers, making goods flow more freely between them.

ww.A treaty in which countries share their: Countries sharing armies is a defense alliance, such as a military pact, and says nothing about tariffs or the exchange of goods and services.
ww.A treaty in which countries raise tariff: Raising tariffs would be protectionism, the opposite of what a free trade agreement does, since these agreements are designed to lower taxes on trade.
ww.A treaty in which countries end all trad: Ending all trade would be a total embargo, while a free trade agreement increases trade between members by lowering barriers instead of removing exchange altogether.

rw: Devaluation is a deliberate decrease in a currency's official value under a fixed or managed exchange rate, which makes exports cheaper and imports costlier.

ww.A ban on using the currency in the natio: A ban on using the currency is a legal restriction on money, not a change in its official value, so it does not describe devaluation.
ww.An increase in the official value of a c: An increase in the official value of a currency is a revaluation, the opposite of devaluation, which means the official value is lowered by the government.
ww.A new design of the banknotes in a count: A new design of banknotes is a change to appearance and has no effect on the value of the currency, so it is not devaluation.

rw: Elasticity is 5 percent divided by 10 percent, which is 0.5, below 1, so quantity demanded changes proportionally less than price and demand is inelastic.

ww.It is unit elastic: Unit elastic would need the quantity to fall by 10 percent, the same as price; here 5 divided by 10 gives 0.5, which is not 1.
ww.It is fully elastic: Fully elastic, or perfectly elastic, means quantity falls to zero from any price rise; a 5 percent drop for a 10 percent rise is far from that.
ww.It is elastic: Elastic demand needs an elasticity above 1, but 5 percent divided by 10 percent equals 0.5, so quantity responds less than price and demand is not elastic.

rw: Price elasticity of demand equals the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price, which shows how sensitive buyers are to price.

ww.The percent change in supply: Dividing by the percent change in supply would give a ratio between demand and supply changes, not price elasticity, which measures how demand responds to price.
ww.The percent change in income: Dividing by the percent change in income gives income elasticity of demand, a different measure, not the price elasticity that this question asks for.
ww.The percent change in costs: Costs affect supply, so dividing by the percent change in costs does not give price elasticity of demand, which relates quantity demanded to price.

rw: Elasticity equals 20 percent divided by 10 percent, which is 2; being above 1 means quantity falls proportionally more than price, so demand is elastic.

ww.10, so demand is elastic: An elasticity of 10 would need quantity to fall 100 percent for a 10 percent price rise; the actual ratio is 20 divided by 10, which is 2.
ww.1, so demand is unitary: An elasticity of 1 would need a 10 percent quantity drop for a 10 percent price rise, but the drop is 20 percent, so the ratio is 2.
ww.0.5, so demand is inelastic: An elasticity of 0.5 would mean a 5 percent quantity drop for a 10 percent price rise, but the stated drop is 20 percent, giving 2.

rw: When many close substitutes are available, buyers can easily switch to another product if the price rises, so quantity demanded is more sensitive and demand is elastic.

ww.The good is a basic necessity of life: A basic necessity of life tends to make demand less elastic, because people must keep buying it even when the price rises, so this lowers elasticity.
ww.Buyers have very little time to react: Having very little time to react makes demand less elastic, since buyers cannot easily switch or change habits in the short run.
ww.The good is a tiny share of the budget: A good that is a tiny share of the budget makes buyers less sensitive to price changes, so demand is less elastic, not more.

rw: For a normal good, income elasticity is positive, because buyers purchase more of it as their income rises, which is the definition of a normal good.

ww.Zero, because demand never responds to i: Zero income elasticity would mean demand does not respond to income, which describes a neutral good, not a normal good whose demand rises with income.
ww.Negative, because demand falls as income: A negative income elasticity describes an inferior good, where demand falls as income rises, which is the opposite of how a normal good behaves.
ww.Infinite, because every buyer spends all: Infinite elasticity is not a sensible description of a normal good; demand rises with income by a finite amount and buyers do not spend everything on it.

rw: An inferior good is one people buy less of as their income rises, because they switch to better alternatives, for example instant noodles or bus rides.

ww.A good whose price never changes at all: A good whose price never changes is a fixed price case and has nothing to do with income, which is what defines inferior goods.
ww.A good that people buy more of as income: Buying more of a good as income rises describes a normal good, so this is the opposite of an inferior good, whose demand falls as income grows.
ww.A good that is of poor quality and canno: An inferior good is not defined by poor quality or being unsellable; it is defined by how demand responds to income, and inferior goods are often widely sold.

rw: Cross-price elasticity shows how demand for one good changes when the price of another good changes, revealing whether the two goods are substitutes or complements.

ww.How prices differ between two countries: Differences in prices between two countries over time describe price comparisons or exchange rate effects, not cross-price elasticity, which links demand for one good to another's price.
ww.How income affects how much people save: How income affects saving is a question about the savings rate and income, which cross-price elasticity does not measure; it involves two goods' prices.
ww.How the supply of a good responds to its: Supply responding to a good's own price is price elasticity of supply, which involves one good and the supply side, not cross-price elasticity of demand.

rw: When one good gets pricier and demand for the other rises, buyers are switching between them, which means tea and coffee are substitutes.

ww.They are complements: Complements would see demand for coffee fall when tea gets pricier, since goods used together move in opposite directions; here coffee demand rose, so they are not.
ww.They are unrelated goods: Unrelated goods would show no change in coffee demand when the price of tea changes, but demand for coffee increased, so there is a link.
ww.They are inferior goods: Inferior goods are defined by how demand reacts to income, not to another good's price, so this does not explain the rise in coffee demand.

rw: Price elasticity of supply measures how much the quantity supplied changes in response to a change in price, showing how flexible producers are.

ww.How much profit responds to changes in t: How profit responds to taxes on firms is a question of tax incidence and profitability, not price elasticity of supply, which links quantity supplied to price.
ww.How much costs respond to changes in out: How costs respond to output describes the shape of the cost curves, which is not elasticity of supply, a measure of quantity supplied against price.
ww.How much quantity demanded responds to a: How quantity demanded responds to a price change is price elasticity of demand, the buyer-side measure, while supply elasticity concerns what producers offer.

rw: In the long run producers have time to expand capacity, build plants and hire workers, so quantity supplied can respond more strongly to a price change.

ww.Costs fall to zero over a long period: Costs do not fall to zero over a long period; inputs always have a price, so this is not why long-run supply is more elastic.
ww.Producers have less time to change outpu: Having less time to change output would make supply less elastic, which is the short-run situation, so this reverses the true explanation.
ww.Prices stop affecting what producers do: Prices keep affecting producers in the long run, and in fact they guide entry and expansion, so this claim is false and explains nothing.

rw: A price floor above equilibrium raises the price so that sellers offer more than buyers will purchase, creating a surplus of the good.

ww.A perfect market balance: A perfect market balance exists only at the equilibrium price; a floor set above equilibrium prevents the price from falling to that balance point.
ww.A shortage of the good: A shortage appears when price is held below equilibrium, as with a price ceiling; a floor above equilibrium has the opposite effect.
ww.A fall in supply quantity: A fall in supply quantity is not the effect; a higher price actually raises the quantity suppliers want to sell while buyers want less.

rw: The more inelastic side bears more of the tax; with inelastic demand, buyers cannot easily cut back, so the price they pay rises most.

ww.Sellers bear most of the tax: When demand is inelastic and supply is elastic, sellers can easily cut output while buyers cannot cut purchases, so sellers bear less of the tax, not most.
ww.The government bears the cost: The government collects the tax revenue and does not bear its economic burden; the burden falls on buyers and sellers through the prices they pay and receive.
ww.No one bears the tax at all: Someone always bears a tax, since the buyer's price rises or the seller's received price falls; the split depends on elasticity, but never disappears entirely.

rw: Consumer surplus is the difference between the most buyers would be willing to pay and the price they actually pay, measuring their gain from the purchase.

ww.The gap between price and the cost of ma: The gap between price and the cost of making a good is producer surplus, which belongs to sellers rather than buyers, so this describes the wrong side.
ww.The total money spent by all the buyers: The total money spent by all buyers is consumer spending or total revenue to sellers, not surplus, which is a gain above what they pay.
ww.The extra goods left unsold on shelves a: Extra goods left unsold on shelves describe excess supply or a surplus of goods in the market sense, not consumer surplus, which measures a buyer's benefit.

rw: Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the minimum cost of making the good, showing the seller's gain from the sale.

ww.The money that producers spend on materi: Money producers spend on materials, labor and rent is their cost of production, not a surplus, which is the benefit left over after those costs.
ww.The unsold goods left in a warehouse at: Unsold goods left in a warehouse are inventory or excess supply, not producer surplus, which measures the gain to sellers from the price received.
ww.The gap between what buyers would pay an: The gap between what buyers would pay and what they pay is consumer surplus, which measures the buyer side, so it is the wrong concept here.

rw: Consumer surplus equals the most the buyer would pay minus the price paid, so 12 minus 9 equals 3 dollars of gain from the meal.

ww.$9: Nine dollars is the price the buyer pays, not the surplus; surplus is the willingness to pay minus the price, so 12 minus 9 gives a different number.
ww.$12: Twelve dollars is the buyer's willingness to pay, not the surplus; the surplus subtracts the price actually paid, giving 12 minus 9, which is 3.
ww.$21: Twenty-one dollars comes from adding 12 and 9, but surplus is found by subtracting the price from willingness to pay, which gives 3 dollars.

rw: Thinking at the margin means comparing the extra benefit of one more unit with its extra cost, which is how rational people decide whether to do more.

ww.The circular income flow: The circular income flow is a model of how money moves between households and firms, and it does not describe weighing extra benefits against extra costs.
ww.The law of large numbers: The law of large numbers is a statistics idea about averages in big samples, and it is not an economic rule for comparing extra benefits with costs.
ww.The principle of advantage: The principle of advantage is not the standard name for this idea; comparative advantage concerns relative opportunity costs in trade, not weighing extra benefits against costs.

rw: The circular flow model shows how money, goods, services and resources move between households and firms through product and resource markets, in a repeating loop.

ww.How a single firm decides its output and: How a single firm decides its output and prices is a theory of the firm, while the circular flow shows the whole economy's interactions.
ww.How taxes move in one direction only, fr: Taxes do not move in one direction only; the circular flow shows money going both ways between households, firms and the government, so this is inaccurate.
ww.How prices rise in a spiral as wages and: A spiral of rising prices as wages and costs push each other up is a wage-price spiral, a feature of inflation, not the circular flow.

rw: In the resource market households sell their labor, land and capital to firms, and in return they receive income such as wages, rent and interest.

ww.Government bonds and notes: Government bonds and notes are financial assets sold by the government to borrowers and lenders, and are not what households sell to firms in the flow.
ww.Finished goods and services: Finished goods and services are what firms sell to households in the product market, so this is the reverse direction of the flow.
ww.Inventory held in warehouses: Inventory held in warehouses belongs to firms and is not sold by households, so it does not describe what households sell in the circular flow.

rw: A PPF is a curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources and technology, so it illustrates scarcity and trade-offs.

ww.A line showing the price of two goods ov: A line showing the price of two goods over time is a price chart, which tracks costs and not the output an economy can produce.
ww.A list of the resources a country owns a: A list of resources a country owns describes its factor endowment, not the PPF, which shows the combinations of two goods that those resources can produce.
ww.A graph of a firm's yearly profit over t: A graph of a firm's yearly profit over a decade is a financial chart for one company, not a model of a whole economy's output choices.

rw: A point inside the PPF means the economy could make more of one or both goods, so resources are idle, underused or used inefficiently.

ww.The economy has stopped producing anythi: An economy at a point inside the frontier is still producing something; it is simply producing less than it could, so stopping everything is not implied.
ww.The economy uses resources at full capac: Using resources at full capacity puts the economy on the frontier, not inside it, so this describes points on the curve rather than below it.
ww.The economy has more resources than ever: A point inside the frontier does not show more resources; the frontier would shift outward for that, whereas an inside point means existing resources are not fully used.

rw: A point outside the PPF shows an output level that cannot be reached with the economy's current resources and technology, though growth might make it possible later.

ww.An output level with no opportunity cost: Every output choice carries an opportunity cost, so claiming a point outside the frontier has none is false; the point is simply unattainable at present.
ww.An output level that wastes resources an: Wasting resources and labor is what a point inside the frontier shows, since output falls short of capacity, so this does not describe a point outside.
ww.An output level that is easy to reach wi: A point outside the frontier is not easy to reach; it exceeds what current labor and machines can produce, so it is unattainable without growth.

rw: Better technology or more resources raise how much the economy can produce of both goods, so the whole production possibilities frontier shifts outward.

ww.A rise in the price of imports now: A rise in the price of imports affects costs and consumption but does not change how much the economy can produce with its resources, so no shift occurs.
ww.A decision to make more of one good: Making more of one good moves the economy along the frontier rather than shifting it, since resources and technology remain the same.
ww.A fall in the number of workers: A fall in the number of workers shrinks the resources available, which would shift the frontier inward, not outward, so this does the opposite.

rw: Economic growth is an increase in the total output of goods and services in an economy over time, usually measured by rising real GDP.

ww.A fall in the number of jobs in the nati: A fall in the number of jobs is a rise in unemployment, which signals a weak economy and is the reverse of economic growth.
ww.A rise in prices across the whole econom: A rise in prices across the economy is inflation, a different concept; growth is about output, not about the general price level.
ww.A rise in government spending only each: A rise in government spending only is a fiscal change that may or may not raise output, so it does not define economic growth.

rw: Rising productivity means more output from the same inputs, which directly lifts potential output and living standards, making it the key driver of long-run growth.

ww.Higher inflation rates: Higher inflation does not raise long-run growth; it creates uncertainty and can harm investment, so it is not a direct driver of expanding output.
ww.A bigger trade deficit: A bigger trade deficit means imports exceed exports, which does not directly add to productive capacity and so does not drive long-run growth.
ww.Shorter business cycles: Shorter business cycles affect the timing of ups and downs but not the underlying ability to produce, so they do not raise long-run growth directly.

rw: Human capital is the skills, knowledge, education and experience that workers hold, which make them more productive and raise the output of the economy.

ww.Land and natural resources of a country: Land and natural resources are a separate factor of production, not human capital, which refers to the abilities that people themselves hold.
ww.Money that people keep in savings accoun: Money kept in savings accounts is financial capital or wealth, not human capital, since it is not a skill or ability within people.
ww.Machines used to make goods in a factory: Machines used in a factory are physical capital, which is equipment, whereas human capital refers to qualities of the workers themselves.

rw: Physical capital is the tools, machines, buildings and equipment that firms use to produce goods and services, and it is made by people.

ww.Shares of company stock held by many inv: Shares of company stock are financial assets that represent ownership claims, and they are not tools or buildings used directly to make goods.
ww.Workers' skills and education, called hu: Workers' skills and education are human capital, which is a different factor from physical capital, which consists of objects used in production.
ww.Cash held by households in their bank ac: Cash held by households is money, a financial asset that is not itself used to produce goods, so it is not physical capital.

rw: The unemployment rate equals the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, which is the employed plus those looking for work.

ww.Unemployed divided by the population: Dividing unemployed by the whole population is wrong, because the population includes children and others outside the labor force, so the rate would be understated.
ww.Employed divided by the labor force: Employed divided by the labor force gives the employment share, not the unemployment rate, which looks at jobless people who are seeking work.
ww.Labor force divided by the unemployed: The labor force divided by the unemployed turns the ratio upside down, giving a number greater than one instead of a percentage rate.

rw: Because a discouraged worker has given up searching and is not working, they are counted as outside the labor force rather than as unemployed.

ww.As unemployed workers: A discouraged worker has stopped searching, and the unemployed must be actively looking for work, so this person is not counted as unemployed.
ww.As employed workers: A discouraged worker has no job, so counting them as employed would be wrong; employed means currently holding paid work.
ww.As part of the labor force: The labor force includes only those working or actively seeking work, and a discouraged worker is not seeking work, so they are excluded.

rw: Frictional unemployment is short-term joblessness while people search for or move between jobs, such as new graduates or workers switching careers, and it exists even in healthy economies.

ww.Joblessness that follows the seasons of: Joblessness following the seasons is seasonal unemployment, found in work like farming or tourism, which is a different category from frictional unemployment.
ww.Joblessness caused when workers' skills: Joblessness from skills no longer being needed is structural unemployment, caused by changes in technology or industries, not the brief search gap of frictional unemployment.
ww.Joblessness caused by a recession in the: Joblessness caused by a recession is cyclical unemployment, tied to falling demand across the economy, which is different from frictional job-switching.

rw: The natural rate is the unemployment that remains at full employment, made up of frictional and structural unemployment but without cyclical joblessness from downturns.

ww.Zero unemployment at all times in every: Zero unemployment is not realistic because frictional and structural unemployment always exist, so the natural rate is above zero even at full employment.
ww.The rate during a deep recession, when f: The rate during a deep recession includes cyclical unemployment and exceeds the natural rate, so it is higher than the level at full employment.
ww.The rate set by law and fixed in every s: The natural rate is not set by law; it results from labor market conditions, and no state fixes it each year.

rw: Cost-push inflation occurs when firms face higher production costs, such as wages or raw materials, and pass them on as higher prices across the economy.

ww.Falling prices caused by weak demand ove: Falling prices caused by weak demand is deflation or a demand shortfall, not cost-push inflation, which describes prices rising because of supply-side costs.
ww.Rising prices caused by too much spendin: Rising prices caused by too much spending is demand-pull inflation, the other main type, so it does not describe cost-push inflation.
ww.Rising prices caused by a stronger curre: A stronger currency usually lowers import prices and eases inflation, so rising prices from a stronger currency is not how cost-push inflation arises.

rw: Demand-pull inflation happens when total demand grows faster than the economy's ability to supply goods, so buyers bid up prices across the economy.

ww.Prices that stay constant despite higher: Prices staying constant despite higher demand does not describe inflation, so it cannot be demand-pull, which involves prices rising when demand is strong.
ww.Rising prices caused by higher productio: Rising prices from higher production costs is cost-push inflation, which comes from the supply side, rather than demand-pull inflation.
ww.Falling prices caused by lower demand in: Falling prices from lower demand describes deflation, the reverse of inflation, so it cannot be demand-pull inflation, which raises prices.

rw: When inflation is unexpectedly high, lenders receiving fixed payments lose most, because the money they get back buys less than they expected when lending.

ww.Borrowers who owe fixed amounts: Borrowers who owe fixed amounts gain from unexpected inflation, because they repay with money worth less, so they are not the ones who lose.
ww.Owners of real estate that gains value: Owners of real estate usually gain when inflation rises, since property values tend to rise with prices, so they do not lose most.
ww.Workers whose wages are indexed: Workers whose wages are indexed receive pay raises that follow inflation, which protects their purchasing power, so they are not hurt most.

rw: The money multiplier describes how banks lend out part of each deposit, which creates new deposits and expands the money supply beyond the initial deposit.

ww.Banks refusing to lend deposits, keeping: Banks refusing to lend and keeping all money in vaults would stop money creation, which is the opposite of the multiplier effect.
ww.Prices doubling each year for all goods: Prices doubling each year describes hyperinflation, which concerns the price level and not how lending expands the money supply.
ww.Governments printing no new money at all: Governments printing no new money describes a fixed supply, whereas the multiplier concerns banks creating money through lending, not government printing.

rw: A reserve requirement is the fraction of deposits that banks must hold in reserve rather than lend out, which limits how much money they can create.

ww.The share of loans banks must make each: The share of loans banks must make is not a reserve requirement; reserve rules limit lending by requiring part of deposits to be held back.
ww.The fee customers pay for opening new ba: The fee customers pay for opening accounts is a bank charge and has no connection to the reserves that regulators require banks to hold.
ww.The tax banks pay on deposits held by sa: The tax banks pay on deposits is a levy, not a reserve requirement, which forces banks to keep funds rather than paying them to government.

rw: The discount rate is the interest rate the Federal Reserve charges commercial banks when they borrow directly from it, usually to cover short-term needs.

ww.The price cut on sale items in a store o: A price cut on sale items is a retail markdown, a different meaning of discount, and it has nothing to do with central bank lending.
ww.The interest rate on home loans from a b: The interest rate on home loans is a mortgage rate set by lenders, and the discount rate is a central bank rate for borrowing banks.
ww.The interest rate banks charge each othe: The overnight rate that banks charge each other is the federal funds rate, a different rate from the discount rate charged by the Fed.

rw: Open market operations are the Fed's buying and selling of government securities to change bank reserves and influence the money supply and interest rates.

ww.Stores extending their business hours at: Stores extending business hours are a retail decision, and the phrase open market operations refers to central bank trading, not shop opening times.
ww.The government selling public land to bu: The government selling public land is a sale of assets and is not how the central bank adjusts the money supply.
ww.Banks opening branches in new towns for: Banks opening branches in new towns is a business expansion; open market operations do not refer to bank locations but to central bank securities trading.

rw: Buying securities puts new reserves in banks' hands, which lets them lend more, so the money supply increases through the multiplier process.

ww.It is unchanged: The money supply does not stay unchanged, because when the Fed buys securities it pays banks, which raises their reserves and lets them lend more.
ww.It falls to zero: The money supply does not fall to zero; Fed purchases add reserves to banks, so the supply of money grows rather than disappearing.
ww.It decreases: A decrease would result if the Fed sold securities and took reserves out of the banking system, which is the opposite of buying them.

rw: The Phillips curve describes the short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, where lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation and the reverse.

ww.The trade-off between imports and export: The trade-off between imports and exports is a trade balance idea, while the Phillips curve links inflation with unemployment rather than trade flows.
ww.The trade-off between taxes and spending: The trade-off between taxes and spending is a fiscal choice, not the Phillips curve, which relates unemployment to the rate of inflation.
ww.The trade-off between saving and borrowi: The trade-off between saving and borrowing is a credit and interest idea, whereas the Phillips curve concerns inflation and joblessness.

rw: A budget surplus occurs when tax revenue is greater than government spending in a given year, leaving the government with money left over.

ww.Exports exceeding imports in value for a: Exports exceeding imports is a trade surplus, which concerns international trade and is a different measure from the government budget.
ww.A rise in the national debt level in a g: A rise in national debt happens with a deficit, since the government borrows more; a surplus would allow debt to fall instead.
ww.Government spending exceeding tax revenu: Government spending exceeding tax revenue is a budget deficit, which is the opposite of a surplus, and the government must borrow to cover it.

rw: Crowding out happens when government borrowing raises interest rates, which makes loans costlier and so reduces private investment and spending by businesses.

ww.Too many shoppers filling a store at the: Too many shoppers filling a store is simple crowding in the everyday sense, not the economic idea of government borrowing affecting private investment.
ww.Firms forcing rivals out of the market b: Firms forcing rivals out by cutting prices below cost is predatory pricing, a competition issue, and has nothing to do with government borrowing.
ww.Banks refusing to lend to the government: Banks refusing to lend to the government would limit public borrowing, which is the opposite of the demand for funds that causes crowding out.

rw: In a progressive tax system the tax rate rises as income rises, so higher earners pay a larger share of their income than lower earners.

ww.Only the poor pay taxes: It is false that only the poor pay taxes; a progressive system actually asks higher earners to pay more, and everyone with taxable income contributes.
ww.Everyone pays the same rate: Everyone paying the same rate describes a flat tax, which is a different structure from a progressive system whose rates change with income.
ww.Rates fall as income rises: Rates falling as income rises describes a regressive tax, which takes a bigger share from low earners, the opposite of progressive.

rw: An automatic stabilizer is a policy, such as progressive taxes or unemployment benefits, that cushions the economy during swings without needing new legislation to take effect.

ww.A rule that bans recessions in the whole: No rule can ban recessions; automatic stabilizers soften downturns but do not prevent them, so this claim overstates what such policies can do.
ww.A machine that fixes prices in the whole: A machine that fixes prices is not a stabilizer; the term refers to existing fiscal policies, not to devices or price controls.
ww.A law passed in each downturn by Congres: A law passed in each downturn by Congress is discretionary fiscal policy, which needs a new vote, whereas automatic stabilizers work without any new action.

rw: Unemployment benefits rise in recessions as more people lose jobs, which props up household income and spending without any new law, so they stabilize the economy.

ww.They fall in recessions and cut spending: Benefits do not fall in recessions; more people qualify when jobs are lost, so the total paid out rises, which supports spending rather than cutting it.
ww.They end when the economy slows down a l: Benefits do not end when the economy slows; they continue and grow as unemployment rises, so this misdescribes how the stabilizer works in downturns.
ww.They raise taxes on workers in the econo: Unemployment benefits are payments to jobless people and do not raise taxes on workers, so this does not explain their stabilizing role.

rw: In a command economy central planners decide what to produce, how much and for whom, replacing market signals with government plans and targets.

ww.Prices guide production decisions in fir: Prices guiding production decisions is a feature of a market economy, where supply and demand signals steer firms, and not of a command economy.
ww.Consumers decide through their spending: Consumers deciding through their spending is a market economy feature, where purchases signal what firms should make, not a command economy trait.
ww.Customs guide who does which job and why: Customs guiding who does which job is the mark of a traditional economy, where tradition rather than planners decides how work is divided.

rw: Competition pushes firms to cut costs, improve products and innovate to win customers, which is a key advantage of a market economy.

ww.Incomes are always equal for all people: Incomes are not always equal in a market economy; rewards depend on skills and ownership, so unequal incomes are a known drawback, not an advantage.
ww.Public goods are always supplied in full: Public goods are often under-supplied by markets because nobody can be charged for them, so supplying them in full is not guaranteed.
ww.Central planning removes all waste in pr: Central planning is a feature of command economies, and even there it does not remove all waste, so this is not a market advantage.

rw: A pure market economy rewards those with money or skills and may leave people with low income without basic needs such as food or health care.

ww.It has no competition at all for sellers: A pure market economy has plenty of competition among sellers, so claiming it has none misstates its main feature, which is rivalry.
ww.It bans private property for all citizen: A pure market economy relies on private property, so saying it bans private property for all citizens reverses its basic principle.
ww.It sets prices by central order for all: Setting prices by central order describes a command economy; in a market economy prices come from the interaction of buyers and sellers.

rw: In a traditional economy, customs and habits decide production, so families passing down farming methods through the generations is a clear example.

ww.Firms compete using prices and advertisi: Firms competing with prices and advertising fits a market economy, where businesses rival each other for buyers, and not a traditional economy.
ww.A government sets quotas for every facto: A government setting quotas for every factory is a command economy, in which central authorities direct production, not a traditional economy.
ww.A central bank sets interest rates for t: A central bank setting interest rates is a feature of a modern monetary system and has no link to traditional economies guided by custom.

rw: An explicit cost is a direct payment a firm makes to outside parties, such as wages, rent, materials and interest, recorded in its accounts.

ww.A cost the firm has long since forgotten: A forgotten cost is not a defined category; explicit costs are clear, recorded payments such as wages and rent that the firm knows it makes.
ww.A cost that never involves any cash paym: An explicit cost does involve cash payment, so a cost that never involves any is an implicit cost, which is the opposite idea.
ww.The value of the owner's own time at wor: The value of the owner's own time is an implicit cost, an opportunity cost with no payment to outsiders, so it is not explicit.

rw: An implicit cost is the opportunity cost of resources the firm already owns and uses, such as the owner's time or building, with no cash paid.

ww.A cost shown on the income statement as: A payment to suppliers shown on the income statement is an explicit cost, so it is the opposite of an implicit cost, which has no payment.
ww.A direct cash payment to suppliers, staf: A direct cash payment to suppliers, staff or lenders is an explicit cost, not implicit, because money actually leaves the firm to outsiders.
ww.A cost that varies with the level of out: A cost that varies with output is a variable cost, which is a different classification and can be either explicit or implicit.

rw: Economic profit equals total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs, so it accounts for the opportunity cost of the owner's own resources.

ww.Total revenue plus implicit costs and ta: Adding implicit costs and taxes to revenue would inflate the figure instead of finding profit; costs must be subtracted from revenue, not added.
ww.Total revenue minus explicit costs only,: Subtracting only explicit costs gives accounting profit, which ignores the owner's opportunity costs, so it does not measure economic profit.
ww.Explicit costs minus implicit costs for: Explicit costs minus implicit costs does not involve revenue at all, so it cannot be profit, which depends on what the firm earns.

rw: Economic profit equals 90,000 minus 60,000 cash costs minus the 40,000 job given up, which is minus 10,000, so the shop earns less than the owner's best alternative.

ww.$70,000: Seventy thousand dollars could come from adding the costs, 60,000 plus 40,000 is 100,000, yet profit subtracts costs from revenue and does not add them.
ww.$30,000: Thirty thousand dollars is only revenue minus cash costs, which is accounting profit; subtracting the 40,000 opportunity cost as well gives minus 10,000.
ww.$10,000: Ten thousand dollars has the wrong sign; revenue of 90,000 is less than total costs of 100,000, so the economic result is a loss of 10,000.

rw: The short-run shutdown decision compares revenue with variable costs, because if revenue cannot cover them the firm loses less by stopping production.

ww.Price against the owner's wishes: Price against the owner's wishes is not an economic comparison; the shutdown rule is based on measurable revenue and costs rather than preferences.
ww.Profit against last year's profit: Comparing profit with last year's profit is not the rule; a firm may earn less than last year and still operate if it covers variable costs.
ww.Revenue against fixed costs only: Fixed costs must be paid whether or not the firm produces in the short run, so comparing revenue to them alone does not guide shutdown.

rw: If price is below average variable cost, each unit sold loses money even before fixed costs, so the firm minimizes losses by shutting down in the short run.

ww.When profit is slightly lower than last: Profit slightly lower than last year is not a shutdown trigger, since the firm could still cover its variable costs and keep operating productively.
ww.When fixed costs are positive and large: Large fixed costs must be paid whether the firm operates or not in the short run, so they do not by themselves justify shutting down.
ww.When price is below average total cost: Price below average total cost means losses, but if price still covers average variable cost the firm can lose less by operating than by shutting down.

rw: Total fixed cost adds the rent of 3,000 and insurance of 1,000 to give 4,000, and these costs stay the same regardless of how much is produced.

ww.$3,000: Three thousand dollars covers the rent only; total fixed cost also includes the 1,000 of insurance, so the sum is 4,000.
ww.$12,000: Two thousand dollars is the difference between rent and insurance, but fixed costs are added together, giving 3,000 plus 1,000, which is 4,000.
ww.$2,000: Twelve thousand dollars would come from multiplying 3,000 by 4, yet no such calculation applies; fixed costs are simply added, giving 4,000 in total.

rw: Average total cost equals total cost divided by quantity, so 10,000 divided by 500 gives 20 dollars per unit.

ww.$500 per unit: Five hundred dollars per unit is just the quantity figure used as a price; dividing 10,000 by 500 gives 20, not 500.
ww.$50 per unit: Fifty dollars per unit would come from dividing 10,000 by 200, which is not the output given; with 500 units the answer is 20.
ww.$5 per unit: Five dollars per unit would need 2,000 units, because 10,000 divided by 2,000 is 5; dividing by 500 units gives 20 dollars.

rw: Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output, so 150 divided by 10 units equals 15 dollars per unit.

ww.$1,015 per unit: One thousand fifteen dollars per unit comes from dividing 10,150 by 10 and uses total cost instead of the change; marginal cost uses only the 150 increase.
ww.$10 per unit: Ten dollars per unit would divide the units by themselves or ignore the 150 increase; the extra cost of 150 over 10 units is 15.
ww.$150 per unit: One hundred fifty dollars is the total rise in cost, not the cost per extra unit; dividing that 150 by the 10 added units gives 15.

rw: Diminishing returns mean each added worker contributes less output, so every extra unit takes more input and costs more, which makes the marginal cost curve rise.

ww.Output prices rise as the firm grows, wh: Marginal cost rises because of diminishing returns inside the firm, not because output prices rise as it grows, which affects revenue rather than the cost of inputs.
ww.Firms forget how to produce their goods: Firms do not forget how to produce; marginal cost rises because of diminishing returns to inputs, so this claim has no basis in cost theory.
ww.Fixed costs rise with each additional un: Fixed costs do not change with output by definition, so they cannot rise with each additional unit and cannot explain rising marginal cost.

rw: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker that sells every extra unit at the market price, so its marginal revenue equals that price.

ww.The firm's profit: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit, not profit; profit also depends on costs, so the two are not equal.
ww.A firm's fixed cost: A firm's fixed cost is a cost figure that does not change with output, whereas marginal revenue is the income earned from selling another unit.
ww.Zero at all times: Marginal revenue is not zero at all times; a competitive firm earns the market price on each extra unit, so it is positive.

rw: A competitive firm maximizes profit by producing where marginal cost equals price, which is also its marginal revenue, because beyond that point extra units cost more than they earn.

ww.Fixed cost equals variable: Fixed cost equaling variable cost is not a profit-maximizing rule, since the firm decides output using marginal values, not by balancing two cost totals.
ww.Average cost equals zero: Average cost cannot equal zero for a firm that pays for inputs, and the output decision is based on marginal cost, not average cost.
ww.Total revenue is smallest: Producing where total revenue is smallest would give poor results, since the firm seeks maximum profit, not the lowest possible revenue.

rw: A monopolist restricts output to raise price, so it usually charges more and produces less than a competitive firm facing the same costs.

ww.A monopolist must charge the market pric: A monopolist is not a price taker; it has market power and chooses its own price rather than being forced to accept the market price.
ww.A monopolist produces at zero profit in: A monopolist does not always earn zero profit; with barriers to entry it can earn positive economic profit over time, unlike competitive firms in the long run.
ww.A monopolist charges less and produces m: Charging less and producing more is what competitive firms do; a monopolist uses market power to raise price and cut quantity, so this reverses the pattern.

rw: A barrier to entry is anything, such as high start-up costs, patents or legal limits, that makes it hard for new firms to join a market.

ww.A fee customers pay at a store to enter: A fee customers pay to enter a shop floor is an admission charge, not a barrier that blocks new firms from joining a market.
ww.A fence around a factory site to keep ou: A fence around a factory is physical security and does not affect whether rival firms can enter the market, so it is not an economic barrier.
ww.A rule that lets any firm join freely an: A rule letting any firm join freely describes free entry, the opposite of a barrier, which makes joining the market hard or costly.

rw: A natural monopoly is a market best served by one firm because very high fixed costs make a single large producer cheaper than many small ones.

ww.A market with many equal sellers and low: A market with many equal sellers and low prices describes perfect competition, which is the opposite of a natural monopoly served by a single firm.
ww.A monopoly created by hiding resources f: Hiding resources from rival firms describes an artificial or strategic monopoly, and a natural monopoly arises from cost conditions, not from concealment.
ww.A monopoly that exists only in nature re: A natural monopoly has nothing to do with nature reserves; the word natural refers to cost structure, such as in water or electricity networks.

rw: Price discrimination means charging different customers different prices for the same good, based on what each group is willing to pay, to raise profit.

ww.Refusing to sell to certain groups of bu: Refusing to sell to certain groups is exclusion or unlawful discrimination in the usual sense, and not the pricing strategy of charging customers different prices.
ww.Charging every customer the same price f: Charging every customer the same price for the same good is uniform pricing, the opposite of price discrimination, which varies prices across buyers.
ww.Lowering prices for everyone permanently: Lowering prices for everyone permanently is a general price cut, whereas price discrimination sets different prices for different customer groups at the same time.

rw: Price discrimination raises profit when groups differ in price sensitivity and can be kept apart so no resale occurs, as with seniors and other adults at a cinema.

ww.Resale between groups must be easy and c: Easy and cheap resale between groups would undermine price discrimination, since low-price buyers could resell to high-price buyers, so this condition would hurt profit.
ww.The seller must have no market power, so: A seller must have some market power to set prices above marginal cost; with none it cannot charge groups different prices, so the claim is wrong.
ww.All buyers must be identical in their ta: Identical buyers would all be charged the same price, so discrimination only works when groups differ, and this condition would remove the gain.

rw: A loss leader is a product sold at a loss, or very low price, to draw customers into a store where they buy other, more profitable items.

ww.The manager who was responsible for a lo: The manager responsible for a loss is not what the term means; it describes a pricing tactic for a product, not a person.
ww.A product that is always unprofitable fo: A loss leader is not always unprofitable overall; the store accepts a loss on one item to boost total sales and profit, so always is wrong.
ww.A product given away for free forever to: A product given away free forever would produce losses without any aim, whereas a loss leader is priced low temporarily to attract customers.

rw: Cost-plus pricing takes the cost of making a product and adds a markup, a set percentage or amount, to arrive at the selling price.

ww.Sets prices by what buyers will pay: Setting prices by what buyers will pay is value-based pricing, which starts from demand, while cost-plus pricing starts from the cost of the product.
ww.Sets prices to the lowest possible level: Setting prices to the lowest possible level is a penetration or break-even approach, not cost-plus pricing, which includes a markup above cost.
ww.Sets the price at what rivals charge: Setting the price at what rivals charge is competitive or going-rate pricing, which starts from the market, not from adding a markup to cost.

rw: A 25 percent markup on 24 dollars is 0.25 times 24, which is 6 dollars, so the price is 24 plus 6, giving 30 dollars.

ww.$6: Six dollars is just the 25 percent markup taken on the cost of 24; the price must be the cost plus that markup, which is 30.
ww.$25: Twenty-five dollars confuses the markup percent with a dollar amount; the markup is 25 percent of 24, which is 6, so the price is 30.
ww.$48: Forty-eight dollars doubles the cost, which would be a 100 percent markup; a 25 percent markup adds only 6 to the cost of 24.

rw: Profit margin is profit divided by revenue, shown as a percent, which tells how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit.

ww.Assets as a percent of equity: Assets as a percent of equity is a balance-sheet ratio of leverage, and it does not measure how much of each sale becomes profit.
ww.Costs as a percent of assets: Costs as a percent of assets is not profit margin; margin compares profit with sales revenue, not costs with the assets that a firm holds.
ww.Revenue as a percent of costs: Revenue as a percent of costs compares sales with spending, which is not profit margin; margin puts profit, not costs, against revenue.

rw: Profit margin equals profit divided by revenue, so 15,000 divided by 200,000 gives 0.075, which is 7.5 percent of each sales dollar kept as profit.

ww.75%: Seventy-five percent would come from a misplaced decimal; 15,000 divided by 200,000 is 0.075, which is 7.5 percent, not 75.
ww.13.3%: A margin of 13.3 percent comes from dividing profit by 112,500 or a similar wrong base; the revenue is 200,000, so the margin is 7.5.
ww.15%: Fifteen percent would be profit over 100,000 of revenue, but this firm has 200,000 in revenue, so dividing 15,000 by 200,000 gives only 7.5 percent.

rw: Break-even quantity is the output at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero, and selling any more begins to earn a profit.

ww.The output where revenue is zero for the: Revenue is not zero at break-even; a firm there sells enough to cover its costs, so revenue equals total cost, which is not a zero level.
ww.The output that earns the largest profit: The output that earns the largest profit is the profit-maximizing quantity, which differs from break-even, where profit is exactly zero.
ww.The output where costs are zero for the: Costs are never zero when a firm is producing, so break-even cannot be where costs vanish; it is where revenue matches those costs.

rw: Break-even equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit; each unit adds 15 minus 6, which is 9 dollars, so 9,000 divided by 9 gives 1,000 units.

ww.600 units: Six hundred units results from dividing 9,000 by 15, which ignores variable cost; the contribution per unit is 15 minus 6, giving 9 dollars.
ww.9,000 units: Nine thousand units treats the fixed cost figure as the quantity; dividing 9,000 by the contribution of 9 dollars per unit gives 1,000 units.
ww.1,500 units: One thousand five hundred units comes from dividing 9,000 by 6, the variable cost alone, but break-even uses the contribution of 9 dollars, giving 1,000.

rw: Selling above break-even means revenue exceeds total cost, so each extra unit adds to profit and the firm earns a profit.

ww.Fixed costs vanish: Fixed costs do not vanish above break-even; they stay the same in total, but sales are large enough to cover them.
ww.Revenue becomes zero: Revenue becomes larger, not zero, when a firm sells more units, so this contradicts what happens above the break-even quantity.
ww.It suffers a loss: A loss happens when quantity sold is below the break-even quantity, because revenue falls short of cost, which is the opposite of this case.

rw: Economies of scope arise when producing related goods together shares inputs such as staff and equipment, which lowers the average cost per product.

ww.Producing less to save paper and other m: Producing less to save paper and materials is not economies of scope, which concerns producing a range of related goods rather than cutting output.
ww.Producing only one good raises cost for: Producing only one good raises cost is not the concept; economies of scope come from making several related goods, not from limiting output to one.
ww.Producing unrelated goods in different c: Producing unrelated goods in different countries cannot share staff, equipment or know-how, so it does not create the savings that scope economies describe.

rw: Selling coffee and bread with the same staff and counters spreads inputs over related products, lowering average cost, which is an economy of scope.

ww.Sunk costs paid: Sunk costs are payments already made that cannot be recovered, and they have no role in explaining shared staff and counters lowering cost.
ww.Price discrimination: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices and has nothing to do with sharing staff and counters across two products to cut costs.
ww.Diminishing returns: Diminishing returns describe falling extra output as more input is added to a fixed amount of another input, not savings from joint production.

rw: The long run is a period long enough for a firm to vary all its inputs, including plant size and equipment, so no inputs are fixed.

ww.A period when firms cannot produce any g: A period when firms cannot produce any goods describes no real time frame; the long run is about flexibility, and firms still produce in it.
ww.A period longer than ten years exactly f: The long run is not exactly ten years; it is defined by whether all inputs can be changed, which varies from industry to industry.
ww.A period when prices never change at all: Prices can change in the long run, and the definition rests on adjusting inputs, so a period of fixed prices is not what the term means.

rw: The short run is a period in which at least one input, such as plant size or equipment, is fixed, so output changes only by varying other inputs.

ww.A period with zero production by firms: Production continues in the short run; it simply limits how much a firm can change, so a period of zero production is wrong.
ww.A period when every input can be changed: A period when every input can be changed is the long run, so this describes the opposite of the short run.
ww.A period lasting exactly one month in to: The short run is not a set length like one month; it depends on how long it takes a firm to change its fixed inputs.

rw: Economic profit attracts new firms into a competitive industry, which raises supply and pushes down price until profit shrinks toward zero.

ww.Prices rise without any limit at all: Prices do not rise without limit; extra entry increases supply, which pushes prices down, so unlimited price increases are not the result of profit.
ww.Firms exit and profit rises for others: Firms exit when they suffer losses, not when they earn profit, so this describes the opposite of what happens in a profitable competitive industry.
ww.Entry is blocked forever by the market: Competitive industries have no barriers to entry, so entry is not blocked forever; free entry is exactly what removes profit over time.

rw: Losses push some firms out of a competitive industry, which cuts supply and raises prices until the remaining firms earn normal profit.

ww.More firms enter the market: More firms entering the market happens when firms earn profit, not losses, so entry is the reverse of the response to continued losses.
ww.Costs fall to zero for all firms: Costs do not fall to zero when firms suffer losses; firms still pay for inputs, and exit rather than lower costs removes the loss.
ww.Prices fall with no limit at all: Prices rise, not fall, as firms exit and supply shrinks, and they cannot fall without limit since firms leave when they lose money.

rw: Profit equals total revenue minus total expenses, so a firm earns a profit when what it receives from sales is larger than what it spends.

ww.Profit equals price divided by quantity: Price divided by quantity is not the profit formula; it makes no reference to revenue or costs and would not measure what a firm keeps.
ww.Profit equals expenses minus revenue: Expenses minus revenue reverses the formula and gives a positive number when the firm has a loss, so it would not measure profit.
ww.Profit equals assets minus liabilities: Assets minus liabilities gives equity or net worth on the balance sheet, which is a measure of ownership value rather than profit.
